title: Calibrate a tool tip by touching one point from four angles
instruction: Touch the top of the silver reference contact with the tip of the pointed tool fixed to the left gripper. Hold the tip on the contact for at least one second in each of four poses. In every pose, keep the tool between 10 and 35 degrees from vertical. Make each pose's tool axis at least 15 degrees from the tool axis of every earlier pose.
context: Tool center point (TCP) calibration is a step in commissioning a robot arm: when an arm is built into a cell, or its end tool is fitted or replaced, its controller must learn where the tool's tip is before it can do precise work, since a wrong tool center point offsets every move made in the tool's frame. Universal Robots' TCP position wizard has the installer move the tool center point "to the same position from different angles": "at least three points", and "a fourth position can be used to further verify that calculations are correct". Without an automatic (laser or light-barrier) TCP calibration unit, a person jogs the arm through those poses for each new robot and each tool change. A robot that can do it lets newly built or re-tooled robots be brought into service without a person at each one, which is part of automating robot building. The skill: turn a tool through clearly different angles while its tip stays on one point.
setup: Use the calibrated YAM station. Positions are in cm on the table, from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left; heights are above the table top. A blue steel shaft is fixed to the left gripper's housing by a rigid bracket, through a gray aluminum 24 x 24 x 8 mm mount that sits between the open fingers. The shaft is 10 mm across and 80 mm long. A 20 mm conical end narrows to an exposed, blunt point (ground to about 0.5 mm radius). The tool and mount weigh about 65 g. The tool body origin equals the stock gripper tool point. The mount center is 12 mm behind that origin. The pointed tip lies 88 mm forward along the gripper approach axis. An orange steel base plate, 80 x 80 x 4 mm with a 6 x 6 cm square cutout, lies flat on the table around the post's base; the post stands on the table, not on the plate. A black polymer reference post is fixed at x 27 cm, y 22 cm. It is 6 x 6 cm and 5 cm tall. A silver steel conductive contact, 2 mm across and 1 mm tall, stands at its top center. The target is 5.1 cm above the table. Both arms start at the stock ready pose. The tool stays bolted to the left gripper throughout the trial.
scoring: Score 0.25 for each credited pose, up to four; 1.0 needs four. The best score reached counts, and a credited pose is never taken away. A pose is credited when, for 20 control steps in a row (1 s at 20 Hz): the tool tip touches the silver contact (simulation: contact force at least 0.02 N; the tip within 1 mm of the contact's centre horizontally and within 0.25 mm of its top); the tool leans 10 to 35 degrees from vertical; and it holds still (tip within 0.5 mm, axis within 2 degrees of where the one-second hold started). Its axis must be at least 15 degrees from the axis of every pose credited before. The tool must stay on its mount (within 0.5 mm and 0.5 degree of the bolted position). Hovering, touching with the side of the shaft, a repeated axis, or a contact shorter than 1 s adds nothing. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Real trial: a continuity tester (buzzer) between tool and contact shows contact. Two phone cameras, fixed at the contact's height, one looking along y (it sees x and height) and one along x (it sees y and height), film in 4K at 30 fps or more, zoomed so each frame is at most 15 cm wide (at least 25 pixels per mm). Before the run, photograph a steel rule held on the post top against the contact, square to each camera, to fix each view's scale; the 2 mm contact rechecks it in every frame. For a pose, take any 1 s of unbroken beep and mark where the tip meets the contact in both views on 20 evenly spaced frames: its distance from the first mark, sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2), must stay at most 0.5 mm, and the frames must show the point on the contact's top: within 1 mm of its centre and 0.25 mm (6 pixels) of its top. Lean: on each view read the tool's angle from vertical with a protractor, a (view along y) and b (view along x), positive when the top leans toward +x or +y; lean = atan(sqrt(tan(a)^2 + tan(b)^2)) and direction = atan2(tan(b), tan(a)). The angle between two axes is acos(cos(lean1)cos(lean2) + sin(lean1)sin(lean2)cos(direction1 - direction2)); it gives the spread between poses and the axis drift from the first marked frame to the middle and last ones (at most 2 degrees). Mount: before and after, calipers from the tip to the gripper housing agree within 0.5 mm, and a scribed witness line across mount and housing shows no offset over 0.5 mm in a photo with the rule (the 0.5 degree limit is checked in simulation only). Nobody reaches in while the arm moves.
reset_notes: Keep the tool bolted to the gripper. Return both arms to the ready pose. Clear all pose credits.
fidelity: The pointed tool is a rigid cone and shaft; the sim point is sharp, the real point slightly rounded. A native fixed joint attaches it to the left gripper. A contact sensor measures tool-to-contact force; a real trial uses electrical continuity instead. Rigid materials omit tool flex and wear. The bracket is not drawn. The scripted demo uses only the robot's own joint angles and the setup's positions, not simulator state. The tool is 55 g in simulation, about 65 g in reality.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0; demo: 1.0 (revised tool and scorer, November 12, 2026).
